en.title: Ocarina of Time Remake Keeps Loading Screens to 'Preserve Essence,' Fans Divided
en.summary: Nintendo's upcoming remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will intentionally feature loading screens, a decision aimed at honoring the original's feel. This move has sparked debate among the game's dedicated fanbase.
en.body:
The much-anticipated remake of **The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time** is set to launch on November 5, 2026, for the Nintendo Switch 2, bringing Link's iconic N64 adventure to a new generation. However, a recent gameplay demonstration has revealed a detail that's dividing the game's passionate community: the intentional inclusion of loading screens.

During a presentation showcasing the anniversary title, series producer **Eiji Aonuma** confirmed that players will encounter loading screens when transitioning between different areas, such as moving from Kokiri Forest to Hyrule Field. "By the way, there's a loading screen whenever you move between areas," Aonuma stated. "This is something we intentionally kept to preserve the essence of the original game."

In the 1998 original, these pauses were brief, necessary moments for the Nintendo 64 to load new environments. While the remake aims for a more seamless visual experience, the inclusion of these brief black screens, marked by a small Triforce logo for about three seconds, is a direct nod to the original's technical limitations and design. This decision aims to maintain the nostalgic feel of the groundbreaking 1998 adventure, a sentiment echoed in other enhancements like contextual jump points and an item quick-swap system.

## A Nostalgic Divide

The internet, as it often does, has reacted with a mix of understanding and bewilderment. For many, loading screens are a relic of a bygone era, an interruption to immersion that modern hardware has largely eliminated. They argue that these pauses detract from the fluidity of gameplay and that a remake should leverage current technology to offer a smoother experience. On the other hand, a significant portion of the fanbase appreciates Nintendo's commitment to authenticity. They see the loading screens not as a flaw, but as an integral part of the original game's identity, a tangible reminder of the N64's capabilities and the era in which **Ocarina of Time** set new standards for 3D adventure games. This decision underscores a broader discussion about how remakes should balance modernization with reverence for the source material.

## What's Next

With the confirmed November 5, 2026 release date, players will soon be able to experience this carefully crafted blend of old and new firsthand. Further details on any other intentional design choices aimed at preserving the original's feel are expected as the launch approaches.

content_raw: Nintendo has confirmed that it intentionally included loading screens in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake to "preserve the essence of the original game," and the internet isn't in love with the idea. Confirmation that loading screens would cut into the remake's playtime arrived during a gameplay demonstration shown as part of today's The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct . It's an extremely brief moment that saw series producer Eiji Aonuma confirm that the Ocarina of Time remake will channel the power of the Nintendo 64 when it launches for Nintendo Switch 2 this November. "By the way, there's a loading screen whenever you move between areas," Aonuma said as Link and Navi traveled from Kokiri Forest to Hyrule Field. "This is something we intentionally kept to preserve the essence of the original game." Let's take a second to break down the footage. In the 1998 Ocarina of Time , as well as so many other games before and after it, loading screens allowed developers to pause the experience and load new areas for the player to explore. With the exception of some cutscenes before and after the original transition between Kokiri Forest and Hyrule Field, players really only had control of Link taken away for a few seconds. The Ocarina of Time remake appears to be a bit more seamless. It's unclear if Aonuma's demo will play out the same as the full release, but here, we see the player in control of Link before a black screen consumes the visuals. It and a small Triforce logo in the bottom right corner are on-screen for about three seconds before Young Link trots back into view. Massive changes to the art style aside, Nintendo's decision to "preserve the essence" of 1998's groundbreaking adventure game seems to mostly line up. That said, in the nearly 30 years since that game came out, players have adapted to an advancing industry that often attempts to hide its loading screens – and that's if a game has them, at all. Nintendo intentionally left some loading screen sections in the Ocarina of Time Remake to preserve the feel of the OG. pic.twitter.com/JBRtLfitq4 — Kabi (@KabiPlays) September 8, 2026 Choosing to intentionally include loading screens in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has players split. While some love the idea of a reimagining that pays homage to '90s N64 gaming, others see the breaks between gameplay as not only a silly addition but a confusing one, too. Some even suspect Nintendo included the loading screens because it needed them on the Switch 2, and not because it wanted them. "Loading times in to preserve feel?" one fan said . "Lol I don't believe that for a second. It's fine that they are in there but don't say that's why you did it, Nintendo."
